summary: This experimental document describes a Path Computation Element based procedure for computing constrained point-to-multipoint traffic engineering paths across multiple domains in MPLS and GMPLS networks. Such paths are needed to deliver multicast-style services over several networks.

eli5.summary: Planning a delivery route that splits to many towns across several countries is hard. This RFC tries a method where a helper computer works out the best branching route.

questions: pce inter-domain p2mp te lsp computation
subtitle: Computing multicast trees across multiple network domains.

tldr.problem: Computing point-to-multipoint (P2MP) paths across multiple domains is far harder than computing point-to-point paths. Existing techniques like BRPC (which work well for P2P) don't directly apply to P2MP because of the exponential branching: choosing the optimal branch point in each domain requires knowing all possible sub-paths from every domain, not just the single best one.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC proposes a "core-tree" approach: compute the optimal tree from the source to the entry points of each leaf domain, then separately compute optimal sub-trees within each leaf domain. This breaks the problem into smaller, manageable pieces while preserving the ability to find good solutions.
tldr.outcome: Multi-domain P2MP paths can now be computed experimentally using PCEP extensions. This enables multicast services (like IPTV or content delivery) to work across operator boundaries, though the approach has scalability trade-offs that may require offline computation for large networks.

today: RFC 7334 remains Experimental. It proposed a solution to inter-domain P2MP path computation with the intent to mature it toward Standards Track after implementation experience, but that transition has not occurred. The exponential complexity of exhaustive path enumeration and the operational challenges of multi-domain coordination have limited real-world deployment, though the core-tree concept remains a reference point for P2MP routing research.

sections.title: The Challenge of Multi-Domain Multicast
sections.content:
MPLS and GMPLS networks use traffic engineering to compute efficient paths with specific constraints, but nearly all work has focused on point-to-point (P2P) paths. Multicast services—such as IPTV, on-demand video, or software distribution—require point-to-multipoint (P2MP) paths that split at various branching points to reach multiple destinations.

Computing P2MP paths within a single domain is hard; computing them across multiple domains (each operated by a different service provider) is far harder. When domains are multiply interconnected (many entry and exit points), the decision of which entry node to use in a downstream domain affects the entire tree. Simply computing the best P2P path to each destination and combining them does not guarantee an optimal multicast tree, and it cannot optimize for overall tree cost or reduce unnecessary domain boundary crossings.
sections.eli5: When one company delivers to many places in its own network, planning is complex. When delivery crosses multiple companies' networks, it becomes much more complex because you must coordinate which gates to use in each network.

sections.title: The Core-Tree Approach
sections.content:
The RFC proposes breaking the multi-domain P2MP problem into two steps: core-tree computation and sub-tree grafting. The core-tree is a single P2MP tree rooted at the source (ingress LSR) with leaf nodes at the entry boundary nodes of each destination domain. The sub-trees are P2MP trees within each leaf domain, rooted at the domain entry node and spreading to the actual destination leaf nodes.

This decomposition has several benefits: the core-tree and sub-trees are smaller than the full tree and thus faster to compute; the core-tree can be computed offline and reused for multiple requests; adding or removing a destination only requires recomputing the sub-tree in that one leaf domain; PCEP messages are smaller since the core-tree path is computed once, not once per destination.
sections.eli5: First, plan how to get to each country as efficiently as possible. Second, in each country, plan how to reach each city. This way, you do not have to think about all countries and all cities at once.

sections.title: Design Goals and Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC specifies several key requirements for the solution. The complexity of computing sub-trees within a domain SHOULD be independent of the domain sequence (which domains are upstream or downstream), depending only on the local domain topology. The number of path computation requests and replies SHOULD be independent of the number of multicast destinations in each domain—this is critical for scalability. It SHOULD be possible to specify domain entry and exit nodes explicitly, to choose branch points, and to reoptimize existing sub-trees. The solution SHOULD also support diverse (disjoint) paths for protection.

The RFC acknowledges that P2MP minimum cost tree (MCT) computation is NP-complete, making optimal computation computationally expensive for large topologies. The solution presents trade-offs: offline computation preserves optimality but requires administration; dynamic online computation allows faster response but may be suboptimal and slower on complex topologies.
sections.eli5: The method should work the same way inside each country, not care about how many cities are destinations, and let you pick which gates to use. It should also let you protect against failures by finding backup routes.

sections.title: Computing the Core-Tree
sections.content:
The RFC proposes using an extended Backward-Recursive PCE-Based Computation (BRPC) procedure. BRPC normally computes single optimal P2P paths; the extension allows each intermediate PCE to return multiple candidate paths rather than just one. Here is the procedure:

1. For each leaf domain entry boundary node, invoke BRPC to compute a Virtual Shortest Path Tree (VSPT)—a set of candidate paths from the source to that boundary node. 2. Combine paths from all VSPTs to form all possible sets (PathSets), each containing one path to each leaf boundary node. 3. For each PathSet, form a core-tree and evaluate its total cost using the specified objective function (e.g., Shortest Path Tree or Minimum Cost Tree). 4. Select the core-tree with the best cost.

This approach requires that all candidate paths flow upstream to the root PCE, which then explores all combinations—a potentially exponential search. To manage scalability, implementations can configure intermediate PCEs to limit the number of paths returned, trading optimality for tractability.
sections.eli5: Ask each country to give you all reasonable ways to reach it. Then try all combinations and pick the cheapest overall route.

sections.title: Grafting Sub-Trees and PCEP Extensions
sections.content:
Once the core-tree is computed, sub-trees are grafted at each leaf domain. The root PCE sends a P2MP path computation request (from RFC 6006 P2MP extensions) to the PCE of each leaf domain, specifying the core-tree path that reaches that domain and requesting computation of the sub-tree connecting the entry boundary node to all the leaf nodes within the domain.

The RFC extends PCEP with a C-bit (Core-tree bit) in the RP (Request Parameters) object to signal whether a request concerns core-tree computation or sub-tree grafting. The RFC also addresses domain sequences: they may be administratively predetermined, dynamically discovered via Hierarchical PCE (H-PCE), or derived from IGP/BGP routing information.

Sub-tree computation algorithms are outside the RFC's scope, but the procedure enables parallel computation: the BRPC for each leaf boundary node can be launched in parallel, and sub-trees can be grafted in parallel once the core-tree is done.
sections.eli5: Once you know the main routes, you send the plan to each country to fill in the local details. Each country computes its local delivery network in parallel.

sections.title: Protection and Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
Protection mechanisms for multi-domain P2MP LSPs include end-to-end protection (computing backup P2MP trees that are node- or link-disjoint) and domain protection (computing a backup tree that avoids a particular transit or branch domain entirely). The core-tree decomposition facilitates both approaches.

The RFC notes several operational considerations. Multi-domain P2MP computations typically take longer than P2P computations, so PCEP liveness detection and timeout mechanisms should account for this. Scaling is a concern: with multiply-interconnected domains, the number of candidate paths grows exponentially, and dynamic computation may become intractable for large networks. Most deployments will likely compute core-trees offline, trading operational flexibility for predictable performance. The RFC also observes that configuration and administration of domain trees across operators can be substantial, particularly for frequent changes.
sections.eli5: You may need backup routes if a link fails. Large networks should pre-plan most routes offline rather than computing them on demand, because computing takes a long time.
